client: I've been really struggling since my mom passed away six months ago. It feels like everyone around me has just... moved on with their lives, and I'm still stuck in this heavy fog that won't lift. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: Thank you for reaching out, even when part of you wasn't sure it would help — that took real courage. I can hear in your words, and even in the way you're speaking, a kind of exhausted heaviness, like you've been carrying this grief largely alone while the world kept moving around you. What you're feeling isn't being "stuck" — it's a very real and valid response to losing someone as significant as your mom, and this is absolutely a space where that pain deserves to be heard.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, "courage" feels like a strong word for just showing up somewhere and talking. It's more like I ran out of other options. But yeah, you're right that I've mostly been carrying this alone — my friends checked in for the first few weeks and then kind of disappeared back into their own lives, and I didn't want to keep bringing it up and being that person who can't move on.
therapist: There's something really telling in what you just said — you've been silencing your own grief to avoid being "that person," essentially shrinking your pain to protect others from discomfort, while carrying it entirely alone. Your voice sounds calm and measured right now, but I wonder if that steadiness comes from having practiced holding this in for a long time. That belief — that continuing to grieve means you're failing to "move on" — is worth gently questioning, because grief after losing a parent doesn't follow a timeline that other people's comfort gets to set.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think you're probably right that I've gotten good at holding it in — I didn't even realize how automatic it had become until you just said that. But I guess I'm not sure what the alternative looks like, because when I have let it out, even just a little, people get this uncomfortable look on their face and change the subject, which honestly makes me feel worse than if I'd just stayed quiet. So it's not just a belief I made up out of nowhere — it's kind of been confirmed by experience.
therapist: You're absolutely right that this isn't just a story you invented — those experiences of people pulling away were real, and they've understandably taught you that expressing grief comes with a cost. I notice there's an energy in how you're speaking right now, like something is surfacing that doesn't usually get to come out, and that makes sense given what you're recognizing. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: those people's discomfort was about *their* limitations around grief, not evidence that your pain is too much — and part of what we can work on here is finding what it looks like to express this in a space where it won't be met with that kind of withdrawal.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and intellectually it makes sense that their discomfort is about them and not me. But knowing that doesn't really make it sting less in the moment, and I'm not sure how learning to open up in here translates to anything different out there in my actual life where those same people still exist. I guess I'm also a little worried that if I actually let myself feel all of this fully, even in a safe space, I won't be able to put it back together again when I walk out the door.
therapist: That fear of falling apart and not being able to reassemble yourself is one of the most common and understandable worries people carry into grief work — and I notice that even as you're voicing it, there's a kind of urgency in your tone, like part of you is bracing for something. What I want you to know is that feeling things fully doesn't mean losing control permanently; in CBT terms, emotions are not bottomless pits — they peak and they pass, and we build that tolerance gradually, together, not all at once. And as for the "out there" question, that's a real and valid concern we'll work on directly — because the goal isn't just to feel safer in here, it's to help you find language and boundaries that protect you in the real relationships where this actually matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The idea that emotions peak and pass is something I've heard before, and I want to believe it, but in my experience this particular feeling hasn't really peaked — it's just been this constant low-level weight for six months that doesn't seem to follow any kind of pattern. And the part about finding language for real relationships sounds good in theory, but I honestly can't picture a version of that conversation with my friends that doesn't end with them getting weird and me feeling more alone than before I said anything.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — soft but quick, like the words are coming from somewhere careful and guarded — matches exactly what you're describing: not a dramatic crash, but this persistent, quiet weight that just doesn't lift. You're right to push back on the "emotions peak and pass" idea, because grief for a parent isn't a single wave — it's more like a change in the landscape itself, and six months in, what you're carrying sounds less like acute grief and more like a exhausting new normal you never agreed to. The fear about your friends isn't catastrophizing — it's pattern recognition — but part of what we can explore together is whether there are one or two people in your life worth a carefully chosen, smaller moment of honesty, rather than a full conversation that feels all-or-nothing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The "smaller moment of honesty" idea is interesting, and I'm turning it over in my head, but I'm struggling to think of who that person would even be — most of my friendships feel pretty surface-level now, like we were closer when my mom was alive and she was kind of the hub that kept me connected to people. And I think that's part of what makes this so heavy, because losing her didn't just mean losing her — it meant losing this whole version of my life that she was at the center of, and I don't know if I've even fully admitted that to myself until just now.
therapist: What you just said — that losing her meant losing a whole version of your life — feels like a really significant realization, and I notice you said it quickly and softly, almost like it slipped out before you could stop it, which makes me think it's been waiting a long time to be named. That's not just grief over a person; it's grief over an entire world she held together, your connections, your sense of place, a whole identity that existed in relation to her. Being gentle with yourself about how heavy this actually is feels important right now, because you've been trying to carry something much larger than most people around you have probably understood.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, it did slip out, and now that it's sitting out there in the open I'm not entirely sure what to do with it — it feels true in a way that's almost uncomfortable, like naming it made it more real instead of less. I think I've been so focused on just getting through each day that I never let myself see the full scope of what changed, and that's kind of terrifying to look at. I don't know if "being gentle with myself" is something I actually know how to do, because my instinct is still to just push through and figure out how to rebuild, not to sit with how much was lost.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with a kind of tightness — tells me that naming this out loud has genuinely unsettled something, and that makes complete sense, because you've just seen the full weight of what you've been carrying for the first time. That instinct to push through and rebuild isn't a flaw — it's probably what's kept you functioning for six months — but "being gentle with yourself" doesn't have to mean stopping or falling apart; it can start as small as just allowing what you said today to be true, without immediately needing to fix it. Sitting with loss and rebuilding aren't opposites — and part of what we can work on together is helping that "push through" strength work *with* your grief rather than constantly running from it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That reframe — that sitting with it and rebuilding aren't opposites — actually lands differently than I expected, and I'm not sure why, maybe because it doesn't ask me to stop being the person who pushes through. But "allowing what I said today to be true" sounds simple and I suspect it won't be, because my brain is already doing this thing where it wants to catalog everything I need to do to fix my social life and rebuild my support system rather than just... staying with what I admitted. I think I've been using the planning and the pushing as a way to not feel it, and I'm only just now seeing that clearly enough to say it out loud.
therapist: The fact that you're speaking so quickly and softly right now, even as you're naming something this significant, feels like a perfect illustration of exactly what you just described — your mind already racing toward the next thing, even in the moment of insight. What you've just identified is genuinely important in CBT terms: that planning and problem-solving have been functioning as avoidance, a way to stay one step ahead of the feeling rather than in it. That's not a character flaw — it's a very intelligent coping strategy that got you through six months of enormous loss — but you've just seen it clearly for the first time, and that kind of awareness is actually where real change begins.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you framing it that way, because "intelligent coping strategy" feels a lot less shameful than "running away from my feelings," even if they're basically describing the same thing. But I guess what I'm sitting with now is — if I've been using planning as a way to avoid feeling this for six months, and the feeling is still this heavy anyway, then the avoidance hasn't even really been working, has it. That's a little hard to sit with.
therapist: What you just landed on is one of the most honest and difficult realizations in grief work — that the strategy you've been relying on to survive hasn't actually been protecting you from the pain, just delaying your encounter with it. I notice there's something in your voice right now, a kind of high, fast quality that sounds like someone standing at the edge of something and really feeling it, even while staying composed. That's not a reason to feel worse about the last six months — it's actually the first moment where the avoidance has lost its grip enough for you to see it clearly, and that's not a small thing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think I'm sitting with something right now that I don't have a word for — it's not quite relief and it's not quite sadness, it's more like the exhaustion of having held something at arm's length for so long and finally letting it get a little closer. And I notice I want to ask you "okay, so what do I do with this" almost immediately, which is probably exactly the pattern we were just talking about. I'm trying to just let it be here for a second, but I won't pretend that feels natural or comfortable.
therapist: What you're doing right now — noticing the urge to immediately ask "what do I do" and choosing to stay anyway — that *is* the work, even though it doesn't feel like anything productive yet. I notice your voice sounds fast and a little elevated, like your nervous system is working hard to hold this unfamiliar stillness, which makes complete sense for someone who's been in motion for six months. That unnamed feeling you're describing — the exhaustion of finally letting something get closer — doesn't need a word or a next step right now; it just needs exactly what you're giving it, which is a few seconds of not being pushed away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
